chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Musa, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali, from his father, from Ali ibn Uqba, from Musa ibn Uqayl al-Numayri, from al-Ala' ibn Sayaba, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'The testimony of the owner of the nard (dice) and the fourteen (pieces) and the owner of the two shahs (chess) is not accepted. He says, "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah," "Died, by Allah, the Shah," and "Killed, by Allah, the Shah," and he did not die, and was not killed.'

key_terms.صَاحِبِ الشَّاهَيْنِ: Owner of the two shahs (player of chess)
key_terms.صَاحِبِ النَّرْدِ: Owner of the dice (player of backgammon/nard)
key_terms.قُتِلَ وَ اللَّهِ شَاهٌ: Kied, by Allah, the Shah (chess exclamation)
key_terms.مَاتَ وَ اللَّهِ شَاهٌ: Died, by Allah, the Shah (chess exclamation)

ai.seo_question: Why is the testimony of chess and dice players rejected in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In Shia jurisprudence, this hadith from Al-Kafi establishes that the testimony of players of Nard (backgammon), chess, and dice is rejected due to their frequent immersion in these games, which leads to negligence of religious duties and the casual, often frivolous, invocation of God's name. The specific mention of 'Shah' (King) reflects the chess terminology where players would swear oaths during gameplay, a practice viewed as diminishing the sanctity of the divine name. This ruling underscores the principle that habitual engagement in leisure activities that distract from piety can impair one's legal credibility as a witness.
